title: Evaluating a new way to provide ultrasound scans in community urology clinics without a specialist sonographer
official: Evaluating the integration of a guided 3D ultrasound imaging system (CUS) operated by non-specialist staff in a community urology setting
summary:
Background and study aims
Ultrasound scans are one of the most common tests requested by NHS doctors, used to check the bladder, prostate and pelvic area. But there are not enough specialist staff trained to do these ultrasounds, so individuals often wait six to twelve weeks or more for an appointment, usually at a hospital. Waiting and travelling are hardest for older people, people with limited mobility, and people living in poorer or more remote areas.

Carrier Tech has developed a portable ultrasound system called CUS (Computed Ultrasound). It is designed so that any trained healthcare staff, rather than a specialist, can perform a scan. With this system, the whole 3D anatomy is imaged and can be reviewed remotely by a specialist. This study aims to find out whether CUS can fit into the normal running of a community urology clinic, and whether patients and staff find it acceptable. If it works well, people could have scans sooner and closer to home.

Who can participate?
Adults aged 18 or over who are attending a community clinic for a urology or prostate problem, and who have been referred for, or would benefit from, a pelvic, prostate or bladder ultrasound. Healthcare assistants, nurses and clinicians who carry out CUS scans or receive CUS reports can also take part by giving feedback.

What does the study involve?
Participants have one extra CUS scan, alongside their normal care. A small amount of gel is put on the lower abdomen and a handheld probe is moved gently over the skin. The scan takes a few minutes. Patients then answer a few questions about themselves and complete a short questionnaire about their experience. Taking part takes no more than 30 minutes, and there is no follow-up. An independent sonographer reviews the images. If the patient also has a standard hospital ultrasound, the two results are compared. Staff taking part complete a usability questionnaire and/or a 30-minute interview about using CUS in the clinic.

The study will measure whether the scans are good enough to be reported, whether patients and staff find CUS acceptable and easy to use, how long it takes to get a result, how quickly staff become competent at using CUS, and whether CUS fits into the clinic’s normal routine without adding extra burden. For patients who also have a standard hospital ultrasound, the study will check how well the two results agree.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
There is no direct benefit to participants, but the study will help decide whether scans like this can be offered in community clinics in future. Ultrasound is safe and painless and does not use radiation. Participants may feel light pressure from the probe or find the gel cold. Sometimes a scan shows something unexpected. If this happens, it is passed to the patient’s own clinician to follow up in the usual way. Standard care is not changed or delayed.

Where is the study run from?
Carrier Technologies Ltd (UK). The data collection takes place at community urology clinics in England.

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
 September 2026 to August 2027. The study runs for 12 months, and recruitment takes place over about 7 months of that time.

Who is funding the study?
The National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) Invention for Innovation (i4i) FAST programme (UK).

Who is the main contact?
Jade Dougoud, jade@carriertech.uk

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Patient participants:
1. Adults aged 18 or over
2. Seeking clinical care for a urology or prostate concern 
3. Referred for a pelvic, prostate, or bladder ultrasound, or would benefit from an ultrasound referral (according to NICE guidelines)
4. Willing and able to give written informed consent

Operator and clinician participants (usability and interview data):
1. Healthcare assistant, nurse or clinician involved in delivering CUS scanning or receiving CUS reports
2. For operators: completion of the study training programme and documented competency sign-off
3. Willing and able to give written informed consent
Exclusion criteria:
Patient participants:
1. Unable to give informed consent
2. Unable to tolerate a transabdominal ultrasound scan
3. Broken or infected skin over the scanning area, or known allergy or sensitivity to water-based ultrasound gel
4. Clinical presentation requiring urgent or emergency imaging, as judged by the treating clinician

Operator and clinician participants:
Unable to give informed consent
